claim: DNA replication is generally followed by DNA mismatch repair (MMR).
source: To avoid mutations in the genome, DNA replication is generally followed by DNA mismatch repair (MMR).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: MMR starts when a MutS homolog recognizes a mismatch and undergoes an ATP-dependent transformation to a sliding clamp state.
source: MMR starts when a MutS homolog recognizes a mismatch and undergoes an ATP-dependent transformation to an elusive sliding clamp state.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure captures MutS in the sliding clamp conformation.
source: The structure captures MutS in the sliding clamp conformation, where tilting of the MutS subunits across each other pushes DNA into a new channel, and reorientation of the connector domain creates an interface for MutL with both MutS subunits.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tilting of the MutS subunits across each other pushes DNA into a new channel.
source: The structure captures MutS in the sliding clamp conformation, where tilting of the MutS subunits across each other pushes DNA into a new channel, and reorientation of the connector domain creates an interface for MutL with both MutS subunits.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and FRET experiments showing DNA movement.

claim: Reorientation of the connector domain creates an interface for MutL with both MutS subunits.
source: The structure captures MutS in the sliding clamp conformation, where tilting of the MutS subunits across each other pushes DNA into a new channel, and reorientation of the connector domain creates an interface for MutL with both MutS subunits.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and validated by crosslinking and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The sliding clamp promotes loading of MutL onto DNA to activate downstream effectors.
source: Our work explains how the sliding clamp promotes loading of MutL onto DNA, to activate downstream effectors.
evidence: This is supported by SPR assays, stopped-flow experiments, and functional assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: MMR is initiated only after detection of a DNA mismatch.
source: We thus elucidate a crucial mechanism that ensures that MMR is initiated only after detection of a DNA mismatch.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data showing that the MutS conformational change is required for MutL binding.

claim: DNA polymerases occasionally incorporate incorrect nucleotides into the new DNA strand during replication.
source: However, despite the polymerase proofreading ability, incorrect nucleotides are occasionally incorporated into the new DNA strand, resulting in mutations when left uncorrected.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA replication fidelity.

claim: MMR reduces the number of mismatches and maintains genomic stability in almost all cellular organisms.
source: To reduce the number of such mismatches and maintain genomic stability, replication is followed by DNA mismatch repair (MMR) in almost all cellular organisms (Kunkel and Erie, 2005; Jiricny, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The initiation of the MMR system is evolutionarily conserved.
source: The initiation of this MMR system is evolutionarily conserved, although in eukaryotes heterodimeric homologs replace the bacterial homodimeric components.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: In eukaryotes, heterodimeric homologs replace the bacterial homodimeric MMR components.
source: The initiation of this MMR system is evolutionarily conserved, although in eukaryotes heterodimeric homologs replace the bacterial homodimeric components.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolution of MMR systems.

claim: Defects in MMR result in a mutator phenotype.
source: Defects in MMR result in a mutator phenotype and in humans in predisposition for cancer, known as Lynch syndrome or HNPCC (Lynch and de la Chapelle, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Defects in MMR in humans result in predisposition for cancer, known as Lynch syndrome or HNPCC.
source: Defects in MMR result in a mutator phenotype and in humans in predisposition for cancer, known as Lynch syndrome or HNPCC (Lynch and de la Chapelle, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The MutS dimer kinks the DNA at the site of the mismatch during mismatch recognition.
source: In this mismatch recognition step, the MutS dimer kinks the DNA at the site of the mismatch and stacks a phenylalanine onto the mispaired base (Lamers et al., 2000; Obmolova et al., 2000; Warren et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: MutS stacks a phenylalanine onto the mispaired base during mismatch recognition.
source: In this mismatch recognition step, the MutS dimer kinks the DNA at the site of the mismatch and stacks a phenylalanine onto the mispaired base (Lamers et al., 2000; Obmolova et al., 2000; Warren et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Upon ATP binding, MutS releases the mismatch.
source: Upon ATP binding MutS releases the mismatch (Allen et al., 1997; Gradia et al., 1997) and travels as a 'sliding clamp' along the DNA helix (Gradia et al., 1999; Acharya et al, 2003; Jeong et al., 2011), and this specific state of MutS is recognized by MutL or its homologs (Grilley et al., 1989; Prolla et al., 1994; Drotschmann et al., 1998; Acharya et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MutS travels as a 'sliding clamp' along the DNA helix after ATP binding.
source: Upon ATP binding MutS releases the mismatch (Allen et al., 1997; Gradia et al., 1997) and travels as a 'sliding clamp' along the DNA helix (Gradia et al., 1999; Acharya et al, 2003; Jeong et al., 2011), and this specific state of MutS is recognized by MutL or its homologs (Grilley et al., 1989; Prolla et al., 1994; Drotschmann et al., 1998; Acharya et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The sliding clamp state of MutS is recognized by MutL or its homologs.
source: Upon ATP binding MutS releases the mismatch (Allen et al., 1997; Gradia et al., 1997) and travels as a 'sliding clamp' along the DNA helix (Gradia et al., 1999; Acharya et al, 2003; Jeong et al., 2011), and this specific state of MutS is recognized by MutL or its homologs (Grilley et al., 1989; Prolla et al., 1994; Drotschmann et al., 1998; Acharya et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MutL proteins are constitutive dimers through their C-terminal domains.
source: MutL proteins are constitutive dimers through their C-terminal domains, while the N-terminal ATPase domains reorganize and dimerize upon ATP binding (Grilley et al., 1989; Ban and Yang, 1998; Ban et al., 1999; Guarné et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The N-terminal ATPase domains of MutL reorganize and dimerize upon ATP binding.
source: MutL proteins are constitutive dimers through their C-terminal domains, while the N-terminal ATPase domains reorganize and dimerize upon ATP binding (Grilley et al., 1989; Ban and Yang, 1998; Ban et al., 1999; Guarné et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: MutL homologs activate downstream repair once recruited by the MutS sliding clamp.
source: Once recruited by the MutS sliding clamp, the MutL homologs activate downstream repair.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the MMR field.

claim: MutL homologs activate nicking of the newly replicated strand by a nuclease.
source: This includes the nicking of the newly replicated strand by a nuclease, which is either part of the MutL C-terminal domain (Kadyrov et al., 2006), or a separate protein such as MutH in Escherichia coli (Hall and Matson, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nuclease that nicks the newly replicated strand is either part of the MutL C-terminal domain or a separate protein such as MutH in E. coli.
source: This includes the nicking of the newly replicated strand by a nuclease, which is either part of the MutL C-terminal domain (Kadyrov et al., 2006), or a separate protein such as MutH in Escherichia coli (Hall and Matson, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MutL activates UvrD in bacteria to unwind the DNA.
source: MutL also activates UvrD in bacteria to unwind the DNA (Yamaguchi et al., 1998), after which the new DNA strand can be removed and re-replicated (Kunkel and Erie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After DNA unwinding by UvrD, the new DNA strand can be removed and re-replicated.
source: MutL also activates UvrD in bacteria to unwind the DNA (Yamaguchi et al., 1998), after which the new DNA strand can be removed and re-replicated (Kunkel and Erie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of MutS homologs (MSH2, MSH3 and MSH6 in humans) leads to mutator and/or cancer phenotypes.
source: As loss of MutS homologs (MSH2, MSH3 and MSH6 in humans) or MutL homologs (MLH1 and PMS2 in humans) leads to mutator and/or cancer phenotypes, these proteins evidently have critical roles in mismatch repair and it is therefore important to understand their exact mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cancer genetics.

claim: Loss of MutL homologs (MLH1 and PMS2 in humans) leads to mutator and/or cancer phenotypes.
source: As loss of MutS homologs (MSH2, MSH3 and MSH6 in humans) or MutL homologs (MLH1 and PMS2 in humans) leads to mutator and/or cancer phenotypes, these proteins evidently have critical roles in mismatch repair and it is therefore important to understand their exact mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cancer genetics.

claim: MutSΔC800 D246C crosslinks specifically to MutL N131C only when a DNA mismatch and a nucleotide are present.
source: MutS D246C crosslinks specifically to MutL N131C only when a DNA mismatch and a nucleotide are present (Winkler et al., 2011; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating that a complex relevant for MMR is trapped.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The crosslinking between MutS D246C and MutL N131C indicates that a complex relevant for MMR is trapped.
source: MutS D246C crosslinks specifically to MutL N131C only when a DNA mismatch and a nucleotide are present (Winkler et al., 2011; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating that a complex relevant for MMR is trapped.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of the crosslinking reaction.

claim: The complex was crystallized in the presence of DNA containing a G:T mismatch and AMP-PNP.
source: We crystallized the MutSΔC800/MutLLN40 complex in the presence of DNA containing a G:T mismatch and the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP (adenylyl-imidodiphosphate).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the crystallization conditions.

claim: The complex crystallized in several different space groups, diffracting to resolutions from 7.6 to 4.7 Å.
source: The complex crystallized in several different space groups, diffracting to resolutions from 7.6 to 4.7 Å.
evidence: This is directly stated crystallographic data.

claim: The same structure of the protein complex was elucidated in all crystal forms.
source: In all crystal forms, we could elucidate the same structure of the protein complex (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2, Table 1), using parts of higher-resolution MutSΔC800 and MutLLN40 structures for molecular replacement.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data and figures showing consistent structures across crystal forms.

claim: The crystal structure shows a novel conformation of MutS in which the subunits in the dimer are tilted across each other by ∼30° compared to the mismatch recognition state.
source: The crystal structure shows a novel conformation of MutS, in which the subunits in the dimer are tilted across each other by ∼30°, compared to the mismatch recognition state (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The subunits in MutS are tilted as a rigid body, but the C-terminal HTH domains hinge around residues 765–766 and move with the opposite subunit.
source: The subunits are tilted as a rigid body, but the C-terminal HTH domains hinging around residues 765–766, move with the opposite subunit, maintaining their role in stabilizing MutS dimers (Biswas et al., 2001).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and supported by citation.

claim: The C-terminal HTH domains maintain their role in stabilizing MutS dimers.
source: The subunits are tilted as a rigid body, but the C-terminal HTH domains hinging around residues 765–766, move with the opposite subunit, maintaining their role in stabilizing MutS dimers (Biswas et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The connector domains are rotated by ∼160° around a hinge at residues 265–266.
source: Meanwhile, the connector domains are rotated by ∼160° around a hinge at residues 265–266, which moves these domains out of the center of the molecule and packs them against the ATPase domains (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1C,E.

claim: The connector domain rotation moves these domains out of the center of the molecule and packs them against the ATPase domains.
source: Meanwhile, the connector domains are rotated by ∼160° around a hinge at residues 265–266, which moves these domains out of the center of the molecule and packs them against the ATPase domains (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The mismatch-binding domain could not be resolved in the density, probably because it is flexible in this state.
source: The mismatch-binding domain could not be resolved in the density, probably because it is flexible in this state.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of electron density for this domain.

claim: The mismatch recognition state of MutS is asymmetric.
source: While the mismatch recognition state of MutS is asymmetric (Lamers et al., 2000), this MutLLN40-bound conformation shows a more symmetrical MutSΔC800 dimer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: The MutLLN40-bound conformation shows a more symmetrical MutSΔC800 dimer.
source: While the mismatch recognition state of MutS is asymmetric (Lamers et al., 2000), this MutLLN40-bound conformation shows a more symmetrical MutSΔC800 dimer.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The MutLLN40 interaction with MutSΔC800 involves two interfaces.
source: The MutLLN40 interaction with MutSΔC800 involves two interfaces (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The first interface is formed by the largest β-sheet of the ATPase domain of MutLLN40 and the ATPase and core domains of one subunit of MutSΔC800.
source: The first interface is formed by the largest β-sheet of the ATPase domain of MutLLN40, and the ATPase and core domains of one subunit of MutSΔC800.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The second interface involves the side of the β-sheet and a looped-out helix of MutLLN40, and the newly positioned connector domain of the other MutSΔC800 subunit.
source: The second interface involves the side of this same β-sheet and a looped-out helix of MutLLN40, and the newly positioned connector domain of the other MutSΔC800 subunit.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Each MutLLN40 monomer interacts with both subunits in the MutSΔC800 dimer.
source: Each MutLLN40 monomer is therefore interacting with both subunits in the MutSΔC800 dimer.
evidence: This is inferred from the two interfaces described in the structure.

claim: The novel conformation of MutS reveals a rearrangement of the subunits in the MutSΔC800 dimer, tilting around the interface formed by the two ATPase sites.
source: The novel conformation of MutS in our crystal structure reveals a rearrangement of the subunits in the MutSΔC800 dimer, tilting around the interface formed by the two ATPase sites (Figure 1D, Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: The tilting creates a new MutS dimer interface of ∼500 Å2 where the clamp domains cross over.
source: The tilting creates a new MutS dimer interface of ∼500 Å2 where the clamp domains cross over, partially from interactions between the helices themselves (200 Å2), the rest from the ends of the clamp domains with the helices.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: Nucleotide density is observed in the ATP binding sites of both subunits in the MutSΔC800 dimer.
source: We observe nucleotide density in the ATP binding sites of both subunits in the MutSΔC800 dimer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and since we crystallized the protein with AMP-PNP we modeled these nucleotides in the density.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density maps shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ATP-induced tilting and increased packing of ATPase domains is often observed in ABC ATPases upon ATP binding.
source: This type of ATP-induced tilting and increased packing of ATPase domains is more often observed upon ATP binding in ABC ATPases, such as ATP transporters, SMCs and RAD50 (Hopfner and Tainer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on ABC ATPases.

claim: A tilting motion in MutS was previously predicted based on comparison to RAD50.
source: Based on comparison to RAD50 (Hopfner et al., 2000) we previously predicted a tilting motion (Lamers et al., 2004), and an open-to-closed transition has been supported by deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (Mendillo et al., 2010), but the crossing of the clamp domains of MutS and the effect that this has on DNA binding were unexpected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An open-to-closed transition in MutS has been supported by deuterium exchange mass spectrometry.
source: Based on comparison to RAD50 (Hopfner et al., 2000) we previously predicted a tilting motion (Lamers et al., 2004), and an open-to-closed transition has been supported by deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (Mendillo et al., 2010), but the crossing of the clamp domains of MutS and the effect that this has on DNA binding were unexpected.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The crossing of the clamp domains of MutS and the effect on DNA binding were unexpected.
source: Based on comparison to RAD50 (Hopfner et al., 2000) we previously predicted a tilting motion (Lamers et al., 2004), and an open-to-closed transition has been supported by deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (Mendillo et al., 2010), but the crossing of the clamp domains of MutS and the effect that this has on DNA binding were unexpected.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The connector domain movement could be the result of binding of ATP in the opposing subunit.
source: Therefore the observed connector domain movement could be the result of binding of ATP in the opposing subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to ABC ATPase mechanisms.

claim: In RAD50, the tilting or 'closing' motion is transmitted through a 'signature coupling helix' via charged interactions with the signature helix.
source: In RAD50 this tilting or 'closing' motion is transmitted through a 'signature coupling helix' via charged interactions with the signature helix (Williams et al., 2011; Deshpande et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on RAD50.

claim: The equivalent region in MutS to the RAD50 coupling helix is only 10 residues long (660–669) and is disordered in all structures.
source: The equivalent region in MutS is only 10 residues long (660–669) and it is disordered in all structures.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The 10-residue loop (660–669) in MutS may be critical for transmission of the ATP signal.
source: It is feasible that this 10-residue loop is critical for transmission of the ATP signal, but the details must be different, since the basic residues in the signature helix of RAD50 are not conserved in MutS.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on comparison to RAD50.

claim: The basic residues in the signature helix of RAD50 are not conserved in MutS.
source: It is feasible that this 10-residue loop is critical for transmission of the ATP signal, but the details must be different, since the basic residues in the signature helix of RAD50 are not conserved in MutS.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence comparison.

claim: FRET increased upon ATP addition when labeled MutS protein was bound to end-blocked DNA containing a G:T mismatch.
source: When labeled protein was bound to end-blocked DNA containing a G:T mismatch, FRET increased upon ATP addition.
evidence: This is directly observed in the FRET experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ATP-induced sliding clamp formation moves residues 449 in MutS toward each other.
source: This indicates that ATP-induced sliding clamp formation moves these residues toward each other, in line with the shorter distance in the new conformation (from 50 Å in the mismatch-recognition state to 43 Å in the MutLLN40-bound structure).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data and the crystal structure.

claim: The distance between residues 449 in the two MutS subunits decreases from 50 Å in the mismatch-recognition state to 43 Å in the MutLLN40-bound structure.
source: This indicates that ATP-induced sliding clamp formation moves these residues toward each other, in line with the shorter distance in the new conformation (from 50 Å in the mismatch-recognition state to 43 Å in the MutLLN40-bound structure).
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structures.

claim: FRET assay shows residue 246 on the connector domain of MutS moving towards residue 798 upon ATP addition after mismatch recognition.
source: FRET assay agrees with residue 246 on the connector domain of MutS moving towards residue 798 upon ATP addition after mismatch recognition.
evidence: This is shown in the FRET data in Figure 2B.

claim: Mismatch and ATP-induced conformational changes open a channel lined by positively charged residues.
source: Mismatch and ATP-induced conformational changes open a channel lined by positively charged residues (left: arginines and lysines as red sticks, middle: electrostatic surface), which would fit a DNA helix (right).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The channel opened by conformational changes would fit a DNA helix.
source: Mismatch and ATP-induced conformational changes open a channel lined by positively charged residues (left: arginines and lysines as red sticks, middle: electrostatic surface), which would fit a DNA helix (right).
evidence: This is inferred from the size and properties of the channel observed in the structure.

claim: FRET assay shows movement of DNA away from residues 449 in MutS upon ATP addition.
source: FRET assay agrees with movement of DNA away from residues 449 in MutS, while approaching residues 336 upon ATP addition as schematically depicted (DNA mismatch represented by pink star).
evidence: This is shown in the FRET data in Figure 2D.

claim: DNA approaches residues 336 in MutS upon ATP addition.
source: FRET assay agrees with movement of DNA away from residues 449 in MutS, while approaching residues 336 upon ATP addition as schematically depicted (DNA mismatch represented by pink star).
evidence: This is shown in the FRET data in Figure 2D.

claim: After addition of ATP, DNA moves away from residues 449 at the DNA-clamp position (FRET/acceptor ratio reduction ∼1.5 fold).
source: After addition of ATP, DNA moves away from residues 449 at the DNA-clamp position (FRET/acceptor ratio reduction ∼1.5 fold), while an increase in FRET/acceptor ratio (>3.6 fold) was observed when MutS was labeled at position 336.
evidence: This is directly measured in the FRET experiments.

claim: An increase in FRET/acceptor ratio (>3.6 fold) was observed when MutS was labeled at position 336 after ATP addition.
source: After addition of ATP, DNA moves away from residues 449 at the DNA-clamp position (FRET/acceptor ratio reduction ∼1.5 fold), while an increase in FRET/acceptor ratio (>3.6 fold) was observed when MutS was labeled at position 336.
evidence: This is directly measured in the FRET experiments.

claim: No substantial change in FRET/acceptor ratio is observed between residue 246 and DNA after ATP addition.
source: Since the connector domain moves down itself, no substantial change in FRET/acceptor ratio is observed between residue 246 and DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the FRET data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The FRET data are in agreement with repositioning of the DNA towards the channel created by the new conformation.
source: Combined, these FRET data are in agreement with repositioning of the DNA towards the channel created by the new conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined FRET data.

claim: The observed MutS conformation in the crystal structure is induced by ATP after mismatch recognition.
source: Based on these validations, we conclude that the observed MutS conformation in our crystal structure is induced by ATP after mismatch recognition.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined structural and FRET data.

claim: The new position of the DNA would allow MutS to fit as a loose ring around the DNA duplex.
source: Since the new position of the DNA would allow MutS to fit as a loose ring around the DNA duplex (with a channel size similar to that of PCNA (Krishna et al., 1994)), consistent with free movement over DNA (Cho et al., 2012), we propose that this is the MutS sliding clamp conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the channel size and comparison to PCNA.

claim: The channel size in the new MutS conformation is similar to that of PCNA.
source: Since the new position of the DNA would allow MutS to fit as a loose ring around the DNA duplex (with a channel size similar to that of PCNA (Krishna et al., 1994)), consistent with free movement over DNA (Cho et al., 2012), we propose that this is the MutS sliding clamp conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to PCNA structure.

claim: The observed MutS conformation is consistent with free movement over DNA.
source: Since the new position of the DNA would allow MutS to fit as a loose ring around the DNA duplex (with a channel size similar to that of PCNA (Krishna et al., 1994)), consistent with free movement over DNA (Cho et al., 2012), we propose that this is the MutS sliding clamp conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The observed MutS conformation is the MutS sliding clamp conformation.
source: Since the new position of the DNA would allow MutS to fit as a loose ring around the DNA duplex (with a channel size similar to that of PCNA (Krishna et al., 1994)), consistent with free movement over DNA (Cho et al., 2012), we propose that this is the MutS sliding clamp conformation.
evidence: This is proposed based on the structural features and functional data.

claim: A loop in Bacillus subtilis MutS was found to be essential for MutL interaction.
source: Recently, a loop in Bacillus subtilis MutS was found to be essential for MutL interaction (Lenhart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The equivalent loop in E. coli MutS is shorter and the explicit residues (F319/F320) are missing.
source: Although the equivalent loop is shorter in E. coli MutS and the explicit residues (F319/F320) are missing, the corresponding region is located within the ∼590 Å2 interface (interface 1) with MutLLN40.
evidence: This is observed from sequence comparison and the crystal structure.

claim: The corresponding region to the B. subtilis MutS loop is located within the ∼590 Å2 interface (interface 1) with MutLLN40 in E. coli MutS.
source: Although the equivalent loop is shorter in E. coli MutS and the explicit residues (F319/F320) are missing, the corresponding region is located within the ∼590 Å2 interface (interface 1) with MutLLN40.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C are located ∼7.4 Å apart in the structure.
source: We created single-cysteine mutants MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C (Figure 3A), which are located ∼7.4 Å apart in the structure, and then showed that we could crosslink them efficiently with a short cysteine-specific crosslinker (8 Å, BMOE), dependent on the presence of both mismatched DNA and ATP (Winkler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure.

claim: MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C can be crosslinked efficiently with BMOE (8 Å crosslinker), dependent on the presence of both mismatched DNA and ATP.
source: We created single-cysteine mutants MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C (Figure 3A), which are located ∼7.4 Å apart in the structure, and then showed that we could crosslink them efficiently with a short cysteine-specific crosslinker (8 Å, BMOE), dependent on the presence of both mismatched DNA and ATP (Winkler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in the crosslinking experiments in Figure 3A.

claim: Only background crosslinking occurred when using MutSΔC800 D246C with MutLLN40 T218C under the same conditions.
source: Only background crosslinking occurred when using MutSΔC800 D246C (connector domain) with MutLLN40 T218C (interface 1) under these conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the crosslinking between MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C is specific.
evidence: This is shown in the crosslinking experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The crosslinking between MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C is specific.
source: Only background crosslinking occurred when using MutSΔC800 D246C (connector domain) with MutLLN40 T218C (interface 1) under these conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the crosslinking between MutSΔC800 A336C and MutLLN40 T218C is specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment.

claim: Several mutants of MutL (A138E, A138E/H139A, R55D/R57D, or combinations) could not complement loss of wild type protein.
source: We found several mutants of MutL (A138E, A138E/H139A, R55D/R57D, or combinations) and a triple mutant in MutS (P595A/I597A/M759D) that could not complement loss of wild type (WT) protein.
evidence: This is shown in the complementation assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: A triple mutant in MutS (P595A/I597A/M759D) could not complement loss of wild type protein.
source: We found several mutants of MutL (A138E, A138E/H139A, R55D/R57D, or combinations) and a triple mutant in MutS (P595A/I597A/M759D) that could not complement loss of wild type (WT) protein.
evidence: This is shown in the complementation assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: The MutS triple mutant (P595A/I597A/M759D) has a slight defect in ATPase activity but this does not impair its sliding clamp formation.
source: The MutS triple mutant has a slight defect in ATPase activity but this does not impair its sliding clamp formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), and other mutants with similar ATPase effects (e.g. MutS F596A) can almost fully reconstitute MMR (Junop et al., 2003), suggesting that the in vivo effect we observe is due to the perturbed interface with MutL.
evidence: This is shown in the ATPase and sliding clamp assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Other mutants with similar ATPase effects (e.g. MutS F596A) can almost fully reconstitute MMR.
source: The MutS triple mutant has a slight defect in ATPase activity but this does not impair its sliding clamp formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), and other mutants with similar ATPase effects (e.g. MutS F596A) can almost fully reconstitute MMR (Junop et al., 2003), suggesting that the in vivo effect we observe is due to the perturbed interface with MutL.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The in vivo effect of the MutS triple mutant is due to the perturbed interface with MutL.
source: The MutS triple mutant has a slight defect in ATPase activity but this does not impair its sliding clamp formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), and other mutants with similar ATPase effects (e.g. MutS F596A) can almost fully reconstitute MMR (Junop et al., 2003), suggesting that the in vivo effect we observe is due to the perturbed interface with MutL.
